subject: anatomy
title: Brain Vesicles, Ventricular Systems and Dysraphisms

steps.tx: During the fourth gestational week, following closure of the anterior neuropore, the cephalic extremity of the neural tube expands into three primary brain vesicles: the prosencephalon (forebrain), mesencephalon (midbrain), and **rhombencephalon** (hindbrain). Two distinct flexures appear: the cephalic flexure at the midbrain and the cervical flexure at the hindbrain-cord junction.
steps.say: In week four, following anterior neuropore closure, the cranial neural tube expands into three primary brain vesicles: the prosencephalon, mesencephalon, and rhombencephalon. Two bends appear: the cephalic flexure in the midbrain and the cervical flexure at the spinal junction.

vis.alt: Primary brain vesicles: prosencephalon, mesencephalon, and rhombencephalon
vis.caption: Primary and secondary brain vesicles derived from the cranial neural tube. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: During the fifth week, secondary subdivision transforms the three primary vesicles into five secondary brain vesicles. The prosencephalon subdivides into the **telencephalon** and the diencephalon. The telencephalon expands dramatically into bilateral cerebral hemispheres enclosing lateral ventricles, while its basal floor differentiates into the caudate, putamen, and amygdala.
steps.say: In week five, the three primary vesicles subdivide into five secondary vesicles. The prosencephalon splits into telencephalon and diencephalon. The telencephalon expands into bilateral cerebral hemispheres and basal ganglia enclosing the lateral ventricles.

steps.tx: The **diencephalon** forms the epithalamus, dorsal thalamus, and hypothalamus surrounding the slit-like third ventricle. Lateral evaginations of the diencephalon sprout early in the fourth week as optic vesicles, which induce overlying surface ectoderm to form lens placodes. The posterior neurohypophysis of the pituitary gland also develops as an infundibular downgrowth of the diencephalon.
steps.say: The diencephalon generates the thalamus, hypothalamus, and epithalamus around the third ventricle. Lateral outgrowths form the optic cups for the eyes, while a ventral diverticulum yields the posterior pituitary neurohypophysis.

steps.tx: The **mesencephalon** does not subdivide, retaining its name into adult anatomy. Its alar plates differentiate into the superior and inferior colliculi of the tectum, while its basal plates form the red nuclei, substantia nigra, and motor cranial nerve nuclei III and IV. Its narrow central lumen persists as the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius connecting the third and fourth ventricles.
steps.say: The mesencephalon does not subdivide. Its dorsal alar plates form the superior and inferior colliculi, while its ventral plates build the red nuclei, substantia nigra, and ocular motor nuclei. Its narrow channel forms the cerebral aqueduct.

steps.tx: The rhombencephalon divides into the metencephalon and myelencephalon, separated by the pontine flexure. The metencephalon develops into the pons and the **cerebellum**, which forms from proliferating rhombic lips bridging the dorsal roof of the fourth ventricle. The myelencephalon differentiates into the medulla oblongata, housing autonomic respiratory and cardiovascular centres.
steps.say: The rhombencephalon divides into metencephalon and myelencephalon across the pontine flexure. The metencephalon yields the pons and cerebellum from the rhombic lips, while the myelencephalon forms the medulla oblongata.

steps.tx: The ventricular cavities contain choroid plexuses that secrete cerebrospinal fluid. Obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow causes **hydrocephalus**. Congenital stenosis of the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius is the most common cause of congenital obstructive hydrocephalus, leading to massive dilatation of both lateral ventricles and the third ventricle with a normal fourth ventricle.
steps.say: Cerebrospinal fluid flows through the ventricular cavities. Flow obstruction produces hydrocephalus. Congenital aqueduct stenosis is the most common obstructive cause, ballooning both lateral ventricles and the third ventricle while sparing the fourth ventricle.

nodes.label: Third Ventricle and Aqueduct of Sylvius

steps.tx: Failure of the fourth ventricle exit foramina (median foramen of Magendie and lateral foramina of Luschka) to open, combined with cerebellar vermis agenesis, causes the **Dandy-Walker malformation**. The posterior fossa expands into a massive cyst-like dilatation of the fourth ventricle with elevated tentorium, causing macrocephaly and hydrocephalus in infants.
steps.say: Failure of the fourth ventricle foramina of Luschka and Magendie to open, paired with vermis agenesis, causes the Dandy-Walker malformation. The posterior fossa balloons into a massive fourth ventricle cyst with an elevated tentorium and hydrocephalus.

left.title: Dandy-Walker Malformation
points: Agenesis or hypoplasia of cerebellar vermis
Cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle
High insertion of the torcula and tentorium

right.title: Arnold-Chiari Malformation
points: Chiari I: Herniation of cerebellar tonsils only
Chiari II: Herniation of vermis, medulla, tonsils
Beaked tectum and low torcula in small fossa

steps.tx: In **Arnold-Chiari malformation type II**, an abnormally small posterior cranial fossa causes downward herniation of the cerebellar vermis and medulla oblongata through the foramen magnum into the upper cervical canal. Almost universally associated with lumbar myelomeningocele, it blocks fourth ventricular CSF outflow, producing progressive non-communicating hydrocephalus and lower cranial nerve palsies.
steps.say: In Arnold-Chiari type two, a cramped posterior fossa forces the cerebellar vermis and medulla down through the foramen magnum into the cervical canal. Tightly linked to lumbar myelomeningocele, it blocks CSF outflow and compresses brainstem nuclei.
